issues.legal_issue: The High Court may review a registering officer’s failure to perform statutory duties when the challenge concerns only the registration process and the failure is gross, even if related civil proceedings are pending or a party was previously directed to pursue a civil remedy.
material_facts: The appellant challenged the registering officer’s act of registering a sale deed, alleging that the officer failed to check whether the purported power agent was authorized to sell and present the deed under the applicable rules.

The appellant did not ask the High Court to determine title or declare the sale deed’s execution void; civil suits concerning the property were pending, and an earlier direction to approach the civil court had arisen from separate proceedings concerning possession.
The registered power of attorney expressly prohibited the agent from encumbering the property, while the registering officer registered the sale deed without checking that restriction.
issues.conclusion: The writ petition was maintainable because it challenged the registering officer’s performance of the registration duty, not the validity of the parties’ execution or title. Pending civil suits and the earlier direction to seek a civil remedy did not oust writ jurisdiction. The High Court may nevertheless decline to exercise that jurisdiction where the procedural violation is not gross or does not shock its conscience.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 permits review to ensure that statutory authorities perform their duties within the bounds of law. A challenge to execution, authority to convey, or title must be brought before a civil court; a challenge confined to the registering officer’s statutory conduct in the registration process is distinct. The Court distinguished Thansingh Nathmal v. Superintendent of Taxes, Sarvepalli Ramaiah v. District Collector, and Satya Pal Anand v. State of Madhya Pradesh, and considered Latif Estate Line India Ltd. v. Hadeeja Ammal, Thota Ganga Laxmi v. Government of Andhra Pradesh, and Amar Nath v. Gian Chand. The availability of jurisdiction is distinct from whether the High Court should exercise it in a particular case.

predicates.is_writ_challenge_to_registration: A party brought a writ proceeding challenging an official act of registering a document.
predicates.challenge_targets_only_registrar_procedu: The party challenged the registering officer’s conduct and did not ask the writ court to determine title or invalidate the parties’ execution of the document.
predicates.gross_failure_to_follow_registration_req: The registering officer’s failure to follow required registration procedures was gross or sufficiently serious to warrant judicial review.

issues.definition: When a writ proceeding challenges only a gross failure in the registration process, the High Court may review the registering officer’s conduct.

issues.legal_issue: A registering officer must check whether a purported agent has authority for the transaction when the applicable registration rules require that check, and must not register a sale deed that the agent’s power of attorney does not authorize.
material_facts: A registered power of attorney appointed an agent but expressly prohibited him from encumbering the property and did not authorize him to sell it.
The agent executed a sale deed in favour of his son and presented it for registration on the basis of the registered power of attorney.
A later, unregistered power of attorney that purported to grant a power of sale was not referred to in or relied upon at the time of registration.
The registering officer registered the sale deed without checking the restrictions in the registered power of attorney.
issues.conclusion: Under the applicable registration scheme and rules, the registering officer was required to check the agent’s authority and should have refused registration of the sale deed. The officer’s failure supported the Single Judge’s decision, which the Supreme Court restored.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 32, 33 and 34 of the Registration Act, 1908 distinguish entitlement to present a document from the registering officer’s enquiry into execution, identity and an agent’s right to appear. Section 34(3)(c), read with Rule 46 of the Tamil Nadu Registration Rules, required the officer to check the agent’s right to act; Rules 48, 49 and 52 address powers of attorney and related duties. The applicable state amendments and rules matter, so the result is not a universal rule for every state. Rajni Tandon v. Dulal Ranjan Ghosh Dastidar does not eliminate the duty to check the scope of an agent’s authority where the applicable rules impose it; Amar Nath v. Gian Chand is not a rule of universal application. The Court also referred to Satya Pal Anand and Thota Ganga Laxmi in explaining the significance of state registration rules.

predicates.is_document_registration_proceeding: A document was presented to a registering officer for registration.
predicates.document_presented_by_power_agent: A person acting as an agent under a power of attorney executed or presented the document for registration.
predicates.applicable_rules_require_agent_authority: The rules governing registration required the officer to check the agent’s right to act in the transaction.
predicates.power_of_attorney_withholds_sale_authori: The power of attorney relied on for the transaction did not authorize the agent to sell the property or expressly withheld that authority.

issues.definition: When a power agent presents a sale document, the applicable rules require an authority check, and the power of attorney withholds sale authority, the registering officer must refuse registration.
